name: Diego Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Diego, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential and won't carry your name. So you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you actually think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I'm into this stuff, so ask away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start with a normal working day. What's it like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter with a big contractor, and right now we're building a huge distribution warehouse off the motorway junction, the kind of place parcels go through. Most days I'm on internal walls, fire doors and the office block at the front. I'm terrible at hanging doors, honestly, Big Martin redoes about one in three. But a few months ago they got a layout robot that drives around the concrete slab and prints the wall lines from the drawings, and I put my hand up to run it, so two mornings a week that's me. I like the early start and the scale of the place, and what wears me out is the walking, I do about twenty thousand steps a day on that slab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would surprise me, honestly. But okay, let's say it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, I got a bit carried away. At work the lads would rip me for weeks, because I'm always showing them stuff on my phone. Online I'd probably post a video of the layout robot with a caption like 'still the coolest thing on site'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much for me. I use AI every day anyway, to plan my week, to look up how to fix my door mistakes, to understand the drawings faster. If that's as far as it goes, I'm still ahead of most people my age on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep running the layout robot, keep using the apps to learn quicker. I'd keep putting money into index funds every month, which I've done since I was twenty-one, so I've got well over a year's wages in there. I'd probably start studying for the site setting-out course next year, because I like that side of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned index funds since twenty-one. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An older guy on my first site told me to put a bit away every week and not touch it. I didn't understand it, so I asked an AI to explain it like I was twelve, and it made sense. I've just kept going since, and now it's the thing that lets me take risks with work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the others on site make of you running the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Priya, the site engineer who showed me how to run it, thinks it's great. Some of the older guys call me the robot's babysitter. But they still come and ask me to mark out their walls first.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, I got a bit carried away. I'd post a video of the layout robot captioned 'still the coolest thing on site'.
S0.think: It doesn't change much because I use AI every day already, to plan, learn and read drawings faster. If that's as far as it goes, I'm still ahead of most people my age on site.
S0.do: Keeps running the layout robot two mornings a week and keeps using AI apps to learn faster. Keeps investing monthly in index funds, which hold well over a year's wages, and plans to start the site setting-out course next year.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little bored by it.
S0.quote: Some of the older guys call me the robot's babysitter.
S0.fieldNote: Diego already has hands-on experience running a site robot, which he volunteered for. His cushion is in index funds he's built since twenty-one, and he links it directly to his willingness to take risks. The plateau leaves him a bit flat rather than relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's more what I expect. Lots of change, not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be young and curious, and a bad time to be stubborn. I'd say it at work in a friendly way, and I'd post stuff about how I use the tools. I'd say the government should help people retrain, but people should help themselves too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The robot I run is exactly the kind of thing that spreads in this picture, and I'm the guy who already knows it. My hands aren't my strongest point, so a job that's more about running machines suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the setting-out and site engineering course straight away, evenings, maybe a year or two. I'd ask the company to put me on more robot work, drilling and layout, and offer to train others. And I'd keep using AI for everything, quotes for side jobs, studying, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your hands aren't your strongest point. Does that bother you, in a trade like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It used to. I came into this because I left school early and labouring was what I could get. I worked out quite fast that I'll never be Big Martin with a door. But I'm good at seeing how a job fits together, so the machine side feels like where I fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone on site who doesn't want to learn this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but don't moan later. I'm not going to push anyone, everyone's got their own reasons. I'd just make sure they knew where to find me if they changed their mind.

S1.say: I'd say this is a good time to be young and curious and a bad time to be stubborn. The government should help people retrain, but people should help themselves too.
S1.think: It's good for me, because the robot I run is exactly what spreads in this picture and I already know it. My hands aren't my strongest point, so running machines suits me.
S1.do: Signs up straight away for an evening setting-out and site engineering course lasting a year or two. Asks for more robot work on drilling and layout, offers to train others, and uses AI for quotes and study.
S1.quote: I worked out quite fast that I'll never be Big Martin with a door.
S1.fieldNote: He's honest that his hand skills are weak and sees machines as where he fits. His views are pragmatic: public help plus self-reliance. He'd help colleagues without pushing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that one I'd have to think about. If it can run the robot too, I'm not special anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and people should get their money sorted now. I'd post practical stuff about saving and spreading your risk. I'd also say the government needs a safety net that kicks in fast, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my head start doesn't count for much if the AI runs the robots itself. I'd have maybe a year of being useful as the person who sets them up, then not. The good thing is I've got money invested, and if AI takes over, the companies that own it will do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move some of my index funds into the companies building robots and AI, not all of it, maybe a third. I'd try to get a job with one of the robot firms setting up machines on sites, because that's where the work would be for a year or two. And I'd save harder, cutting the motorbike trips and the gadgets, so I'd have a bigger pile for when the work stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I had options, but the clock would be really loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the companies that own it will do well. Does it bother you to bet on the thing replacing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. My mum would say it's like betting on the fox. But if it's happening either way, I'd rather have some of the upside than none. I'm not going to change what happens by keeping my money in a savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Martin. He's brilliant with his hands and he hates phones. He's got a mortgage and two teenagers. I don't think two years is enough for him to do anything except worry.

S2.say: I'd say it's going to be rough and people should sort their money out now. The government needs a safety net that kicks in fast, because two years is nothing.
S2.think: My head start doesn't count for much if the AI runs the robots itself, so I'd have maybe a year of being useful. But my money's invested, and the companies that own the AI will do well.
S2.do: Moves about a third of his index funds into robot and AI companies. Tries to get a job with a robot firm setting up machines on sites, and saves harder by cutting motorbike trips and gadgets.
S2.feel: Anxious but still with options, with the clock sounding very loud.
S2.quote: My mum would say it's like betting on the fox.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture strips away his advantage, and he says so quickly. He responds like an investor, putting part of his money behind the technology while feeling uneasy about it. He thinks of Big Martin, whose life stage makes him far more exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to plan, not panic. Learn the tools, get your savings sorted, think about what you'd do next. I'd be posting a lot about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is about right for me. I'd get properly qualified in site engineering and spend a few years running robot crews, which would pay well. When it goes all the way, I'd have more saved and invested, and I'd still be in my early thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the site engineering course in the first year and push to run robot work on every job. Around year two, I'd move to a robot firm or a contractor that's all-in on automation, for better pay. I'd keep shifting a bit more of my investments towards AI and robot companies each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in a good way. Like before a big exam you've studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'when it goes all the way.' What do you picture doing then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. Maybe nothing for a while, living off the investments if they've done well. Maybe something with people, I don't know. I'd rather not pretend I've got that bit figured out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years give you that the two-year version didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to make the head start count. In two years I'm just scrambling to grab a job at a robot firm. In five, I can actually be good at it and earn and save before it changes again.

S3.say: I'd say this is a chance to plan, not panic: learn the tools, sort your savings, think about what's next. I'd post about it a lot, probably too much.
S3.think: Five years is about right for me: get qualified, run robot crews for a few years on good pay. When it goes all the way, I'd have more saved and still be in my early thirties.
S3.do: Takes the site engineering course in the first year and pushes to run robot work on every job. Moves around year two to a robot firm or heavily automated contractor for better pay, and shifts more investments towards AI and robot companies each year.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a mostly good way, like before an exam he's studied for.
S3.quote: I'd rather not pretend I've got that bit figured out.
S3.fieldNote: He sees the five-year version as the best fit for his head start, turning it into earnings and savings. He's honest that he has no plan for after full AGI. He expects his investments, not his work, to carry him eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to get ready if they start now. I'd say it to the lads on site, and I'd be pushing the company to train people properly. Online I'd be the guy saying, don't wait till year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one is good for me. Ten years is a whole career of being the guy who knows the machines. I'd earn well, invest steadily, and by the end I wouldn't need a job in the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the site engineering course and maybe a robotics course after that. I'd start a small side business teaching other contractors to set up and run layout robots, because small firms will want that and won't know where to start. I'd keep investing every month, a bit more each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel like I had time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said your mum would call investing in AI betting on the fox. Would you tell her to do the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to think about it, but she won't. She keeps her money under the mattress, basically. I'd probably just make sure I've got enough to help her if she needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will waste it. Ten years sounds like forever, so half the lads on site will do nothing until year eight. I can already see it, and I can't really do anything about it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to get ready if they start now. Online I'd be the guy saying don't wait till year nine.
S4.think: Ten years is a whole career of being the guy who knows the machines. I'd earn well, invest steadily and by the end wouldn't need a job in the same way.
S4.do: Takes the site engineering course and then a robotics course. Starts a small side business teaching other contractors to set up and run layout robots, and raises his monthly investment a little each year.
S4.feel: Calm, with time to get it right.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever, so half the lads on site will do nothing until year eight.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he's confident and sees a business in helping small firms. His concern shifts from himself to others who will waste the time. He plans to support his mum rather than change her habits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my head start would be gone before I could use it. What would help is a safety net that kicks in fast, not in a year, and short courses that are actually free for people who need to switch quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the money matters. I can say all this calmly because I've got savings. If I didn't, I'd probably sound a lot more like the guys who are scared. Being chill about this is kind of a luxury.

headlineQuote: Being chill about this is kind of a luxury.
portrait: Diego Yilmaz is a 27-year-old junior carpenter at a large contractor, poor at hanging doors but quick to volunteer for the site's layout robot, and he uses AI every day. He's invested in index funds since he was twenty-one and openly links that cushion to his calm. He's relaxed or even excited through the milder pictures and plans to move into site engineering and robot work. The fast AGI picture makes him anxious because it wipes out his head start, so he'd bet part of his money on robot companies. With more time he plans to make his head start pay, though he admits he has no plan for after full AGI.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his head start with the robots would be gone before he could make use of it.
whatWouldHelp: A safety net that kicks in fast, and short, free courses for people who need to switch work quickly.
